summary: This memo outlines high-level requirements for adding Mandatory Access Control to NFSv4.2. It describes the protections to be offered over protocol components and the basic structure of the proposed system.

eli5.summary: Files may have secret stickers saying who may read them. This lists what the sharing system must do to carry those stickers.

subtitle: What NFS needs in order to carry security labels so mandatory access control works over the network.

tldr.problem: Mandatory access control systems label files and processes, but NFS had no way to transfer, store and enforce those labels between clients and servers.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists requirements for Labeled NFS: label transport and storage tagged with a Label Format Specifier, protected by authentication, integrity and privacy, with policy enforced by the client and, where able, the server, in three modes of operation.
tldr.outcome: It records requirements and use cases for NFSv4.2 labeling, from diskless Linux to multi-level security, without itself defining the protocol.

today: RFC 7204 is an Informational requirements document and has not been obsoleted or updated. It lists what Labeled NFS must do; the protocol itself is not defined here.

sections.title: MAC Versus DAC
sections.content:
Mandatory Access Control (MAC) systems are mainstream in operating systems such as Linux, FreeBSD and Solaris. They bind security attributes to subjects (processes) and objects, and use them to decide access. Unix permissions and ACLs are Discretionary Access Control (DAC): decisions rest on user identity and ownership, and users set rules for what they own.

MAC decisions instead rest on the labels of subject and object under a system-wide policy that users cannot override. A DAC user can still run flawed software with full user permissions, while MAC can confine it at a finer granularity. The document records requirements, and the client constraints imposed by existing security models, to help people outside the NFS community understand them.
sections.eli5: With normal rules the owner decides who may touch a file. With labels, the school principal sets the rules for everyone and even owners cannot change them.

sections.title: Key Definitions
sections.content:
A Label Format Specifier (LFS) identifies the syntax of a security label and the meaning of its parts; an optional Policy Identifier names specific policies. A foreign label is in a format other than the one a MAC implementation uses.

A MAC-Aware server can transmit and store object labels. A MAC-Functional client or server is Labeled NFS enabled and can interpret labels and apply policy. Multi-Level Security (MLS) gives objects a sensitivity level such as Unclassified, Secret or Top Secret. The RFC uses the keywords MUST, SHOULD and MAY as in RFC 2119.
sections.eli5: A label format is like the language the sticker is written in. Some computers only store stickers, and others actually read them and follow the rules.

sections.title: The Requirements
sections.content:
General requirements: clients MUST convey the subject's privileges to the server; servers MUST store and retrieve security attributes of exported files; servers MUST notify clients of attribute changes; and clients and servers MUST negotiate label formats and translate between them.

All NFSv4.2 messaging MUST have authentication, integrity and privacy, configurable per policy, with strong mutual authentication for Full Mode. Labels MUST be tagged with a valid LFS, and a system MUST reject any label with an LFS it does not recognize. A label MUST mean exactly the same on every system within one MAC model, and implementations MUST validate labels received from a peer.

On creation, the client computes the label from its policy and the server may deny it, but MUST bind the label to the object before the object becomes visible. The server SHOULD NOT invent a different label and MUST NOT change a label's semantic meaning when translating. The client MUST apply its own policy using labels from the server, be configurable for how long it caches label state, and flush state if server policy changes. A MAC-Functional server MUST enforce policy on local and remote operations, and SHOULD recall a delegation if the label changes. If an existing server is upgraded, the security system defines behavior for existing unlabeled objects.
sections.eli5: The rules say: the sticker must be kept safe in transit, always written in a language both sides understand, and checked by whoever can check it. If nobody understands a sticker, it is refused.

sections.title: Three Modes of Operation
sections.content:
In Full Mode both sides are MAC-Functional. On first lookup the client sends the process security context, the server checks policy and releases the object with its security information, and then the client checks its own policy. Later, with a handle, the order reverses so the client can avoid requests that would fail anyway.

In Limited Server Mode the server is MAC-Aware and the clients are MAC-Functional. The server can store and transmit labels but cannot enforce them, and MUST tell clients when the label of a file they have open changes. In Guest Mode only one side is MAC-Functional, and it is standard NFSv4.2 over the wire; the MAC-Functional side maps the other side's processes or objects to labels using other characteristics.
sections.eli5: Sometimes both computers read the stickers. Sometimes only one stores them and the other does the checking. Sometimes only one of them cares about stickers at all and it guesses the rest.

sections.title: Use Cases and Multi-Level Security
sections.content:
The use cases are full MAC labeling of remotely mounted file systems, such as home directories protected from malicious web scripts; MAC labeling of virtual machine images stored on the network; simple security label storage in mixed networks; and diskless Linux, where labels define policy that standard NFS ACLs cannot express.

The MLS example uses Unclassified, Secret and Top Secret. A process labeled Secret cannot read a Top Secret directory because its level does not dominate the directory's, so the client's MAC module denies it. A Top Secret process passes the client check, and the server then checks too. The server may add constraints: if a subnet is cleared only up to Secret, the same request fails at the server. With a MAC-Functional server only, the server labels requests by subnet and returns NFS4ERR_ACCESS.
sections.eli5: A kid with a Secret badge cannot walk into a Top Secret room. The classroom door checks the badge, and the building door checks again, and either one can say no.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Labeled NFS is a way to transport and store labels and to interpret them, not a set of policies. It does not say whether a MAC-Functional client can demand that a MAC-Aware server accept only MAC-Functional clients. That is a policy, which a MAC model can supply, for example a new LFS that forbids non-MAC-Functional clients.

In Guest Mode one side does not enforce MAC protections, so threats from tampering outside the alternate methods must be identified and mitigated. For MAC-Functional clients, a single client that skips its access checks would violate the model.
sections.eli5: The sticker system only works if every computer plays by the rules. If one computer ignores stickers, the whole system is weaker.
